title: HIIT Workouts Can Reverse Cellular Aging by Nearly a Decade, Studies Show
excerpt: Multiple peer-reviewed studies find that high-intensity interval training boosts mitochondrial function, lengthens telomeres, and rolls back biological age markers in adults over 65.
body:
• A Mayo Clinic study found HIIT boosted mitochondrial capacity by 69% in adults over 65, reversing age-related cellular decline that no medication can replicate.
  • Researchers at Loma Linda University showed that just 12 HIIT sessions over four weeks reduced biological age by 3.59 years in sedentary adults aged 40–65.
  • A six-month European Heart Journal trial found HIIT and endurance training increased telomerase activity two- to three-fold, while resistance training alone did not.
  • Brigham Young University data from nearly 6,000 adults linked high-intensity exercise to telomeres with a nine-year biological aging advantage over sedentary lifestyles.

A growing body of peer-reviewed research points to one exercise modality as the closest thing science has to an anti-aging prescription: high-intensity interval training. Multiple studies now show that HIIT—short bursts of all-out effort alternating with brief recovery periods—can reverse cellular aging markers by seven to nine years in adults who stick with it.

The findings arrive as metabolic disease and sedentary lifestyles accelerate biological aging across populations worldwide, making the case for HIIT not just a fitness trend but a public-health imperative.

The Mayo Clinic Discovery

The landmark study came in 2017, when researchers at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, published results in Cell Metabolism that stunned the exercise science community. The team, led by senior author Dr. K. Sreekumaran Nair, enrolled 72 men and women in two age groups—18 to 30 and 65 to 80—and assigned them to 12 weeks of HIIT cycling, weight training, or a combination of both.

All three programs improved lean body mass and insulin sensitivity. But only HIIT produced dramatic cellular results. In adults over 65, mitochondrial respiration—the process by which cells convert nutrients into energy—jumped 69%. Younger participants saw a 49% increase. Resistance training alone produced no comparable mitochondrial benefit.

"Based on everything we know, there's no substitute for these exercise programs when it comes to delaying the aging process. These things we are seeing cannot be done by any medicine."

— Dr. K. Sreekumaran Nair, Mayo Clinic endocrinologist and diabetes researcher

The study also found that HIIT enhanced the cellular machinery responsible for manufacturing new proteins, effectively reversing a hallmark of aging at the molecular level. Dr. Nair cautioned, however, that building muscle strength still requires adding resistance training two to three days per week.

Biological Age Rolled Back in Weeks

More recent research has reinforced these findings with even more striking timelines. A 2023 randomized controlled trial from Loma Linda University, published in Aging Cell, found that just four weeks of HIIT reduced transcriptomic age—a gene-expression-based measure of biological aging—by 3.59 years in sedentary adults aged 40 to 65.

The protocol was remarkably modest: three sessions per week, each lasting only 23 minutes, for a total of 276 minutes of exercise over the entire month. Participants alternated between rowing, cycling, and treadmill work at 77% to 93% of their predicted maximum heart rate. The control group, which did not exercise, saw their transcriptomic age increase by 3.29 years over the same period.

A separate study published in the European Heart Journal tracked 124 healthy, previously inactive middle-aged adults over six months. Those assigned to HIIT or endurance training saw telomerase activity—the enzyme that repairs and lengthens telomeres—increase two- to three-fold. Telomere length, the nucleotide caps on chromosomes that shorten with age, also grew in the endurance-trained groups. Resistance training produced no such telomere benefits.

The Telomere Connection

Telomeres function as biological clocks. Each time a cell divides, these protective chromosome endcaps shorten slightly. When they get too short, cells stop functioning properly or die. Brigham Young University exercise scientist Larry Tucker analysed data from nearly 6,000 adults aged 20 to 84, publishing his findings in Preventive Medicine.

Tucker found that adults with consistently high physical activity levels had telomeres with a nine-year biological aging advantage over sedentary peers, and a seven-year advantage over moderately active individuals. To qualify as "highly active," women needed 30 minutes of jogging per day, five days a week; men needed 40 minutes.

"If you want to see a real difference in slowing your biological aging, it appears that a little exercise won't cut it. You have to work out regularly at high levels."

— Larry Tucker, exercise science professor, Brigham Young University

What Makes HIIT Different

HIIT typically involves intense work intervals of 15 seconds to four minutes at 80% to 95% of maximum heart rate, followed by equal or slightly longer recovery periods at lower intensity. A full session can last as little as 10 to 23 minutes—a fraction of the time required for endurance training, which often demands 30 to 60 minutes of continuous effort.

A Canadian study found that sedentary men who performed just 10 minutes of sprint intervals three times per week achieved cardiometabolic improvements equal to those doing 50 minutes of continuous exercise, after 12 weeks. This time efficiency is a major factor in HIIT's growing adoption, according to a 2025 review published in ScienceDaily that found physical fitness is "closely associated with slower epigenetic aging" across multiple organs including the heart, liver, and skeletal muscle.

Researchers noted that even Olympic athletes showed measurably slower epigenetic aging than non-athletes, suggesting that the benefits of sustained high-intensity training accumulate over a lifetime.

Starting a HIIT Program Safely

Experts recommend that beginners start with a physician's clearance, particularly adults over 50 or those with cardiovascular risk factors. A basic beginner protocol might include three rounds of 45 seconds of bodyweight exercises—push-ups, squats, high kicks, and jumping jacks—followed by 15-second rest periods, totaling roughly 10 minutes.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends strength training at least two days per week alongside aerobic activity. Dr. Nair's research supports combining HIIT with resistance work: interval training delivers the mitochondrial and cardiovascular benefits, while weights build the muscle mass that HIIT alone cannot fully provide.

More than 25% of Americans engage in no physical activity outside of work, according to the CDC. A 2020 European Union study found 53% of adults spent more than 4.5 hours per day sedentary. The research suggests that even small doses of high-intensity exercise can produce outsized biological returns—a message that may be especially relevant as India's urban population grapples with rising rates of diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
